newsitem.title: USA: Dole, Clinton hold stinging final debate.
newsitem.headline: Dole, Clinton hold stinging final debate.

text.p: Bob Dole accused President Bill Clinton of presiding over "ethical scandals in the White House" and Clinton rapped Dole as a man of outmoded ideas and empty promises on Wednesday in a campaign debate full of stinging exchanges.

As expected, Republican nominee Dole lashed out at Clinton's ethics, credibility and performance and the president parried coolly -- even affably at times -- in a second, 90-minute televised contest that shaped up as Dole's last chance to slow Clinton's re-election bandwagon.

The clash less than three weeks before the Nov. 5 election was odd in that the sometimes insulting cut-and-thrust was presented in a clubby, even-tempered style by rivals who tiptoed around each other on a stage as they talked and came across like debating's version of Alfonse-and-Gaston in matching dark blue suits.

As in the first debate on Oct. 6, Dole gave a good account of himself but so did Clinton, and it seemed unlikely the challenger had scored the big public opinion breakthrough he needed to overcome Clinton's commanding polling leads.
Snap polls taken by television networks right after the debate suggested Clinton was the winner.
Dole's main thrust was to paint Clinton as an untrustworthy high-taxing liberal with a blind eye to staff scandal, and he drove it home with chopping broadsides.
"My word is good, I keep my promises, I don't break my promises after the election," he said in one typical assertion that Clinton had broken a promise to cut middle-class taxes.
Clinton's strategy was to rebut calmly and try to make Dole's charges seem desperate and exaggerated.

"No attack ever created a job or educated a child or helped a family make ends meet," he said in a typical comment. "No insult ever cleaned up a toxic waste dump or helped an elderly person. And ... that's what I've worked on."
Dole, urged to hit Clinton on ethical issues where Republicans think him vulnerable, lunged to the attack in his reply to a question only marginally connected with that issue.
He said many Americans had lost faith in government because "they see ethical scandals in the White House today."

He referred specifically to the collection of FBI files by Clinton White House security aides in the president's first year in office, and to reports Clinton might be considering a presidential pardon for former business associates convicted of fraud in Arkansas in the Whitewater affair.
"I think now that (the public) trust is being violated. The president should say tonight he is not going to pardon anybody who was in business with him who might implicate him later on," Dole said.

Dole returned to that line of attack later in the debate as well and Clinton handled both assaults by ignoring them and commenting instead on what he saw as the positive aspects of his four years in officer.

"This is a real important election ... and the decisions we make will have real important consequences," he said in his closing statement. He told the audience they, the voters, would decide whether America would balance its budget, give fair tax cuts "and build a bridge to the 21sdt century."

He was set on brushing off Dole's broadsides and accentuating his record, saying at the outset: "Compared to four years ago, we're clearly better off. We've got 10.5 million more jobs. The deficit's been reduced by 60 percent. Incomes are rising for the first time in a decade."

Dole insisted there was widespread economic unease among working people despite the overall positive economic figures, and insisted people yearned for his promised 15 percent tax cut after what he claimed were unrivaled Clinton tax hikes.
Clinton scoffed at Dole's insistence he could cut taxes and balance the budget simultaneously, saying this idea had been repudiated by Nobel Prize-winning economists.
The debate questions were all posed by a panel of 113 undecided voters gathered by random polling in a university theater in this Pacific Coast seaport.

They provoked sharp disputes on questions of interest to average votersa -- such as welfare reform, illegal immigration problems and affirmative action equal-rights policies -- and also brought on a lighter moment when Dole was asked about concerns he was too old at 73 to be president.

"Well, wisdom comes from age, experience and intelligence. And if you have some of each -- and I have some age, some experience, some intelligence -- that adds up to wisdom," Dole said in a reply that drew an appreciative chuckle from the audience and a smile from Clinton as well.
But it also gave Clinton a chance to get in an uppercut, which he did by saying, "I don't think Senator Dole is too old to be president. It's the age of his ideas that I question."
Both Dole and Clinton declined to speak from the podiums provided and moved about the stage gesticulating and directing their answers to members of the audience.
Once they almost collided as they moved to center stage, and Dole stepped back, saying, "I'll get out of your way."
He also challenged Clinton to another debate at one point. Clinton ignored that sally, too.
